c.tagline: Sahelian riverside capital where the Niger River meets the desert.

taxi.color: green/yellow shared taxis, unmarked private taxis
taxi.fareNote: No meters are used; agree on or confirm the fixed fare with the driver before the ride starts. Shared city taxis run fixed low-cost routes; private/full-ride taxis cost more and require negotiation.

emergency.note: Fire: 18. Response times can be slow and dispatchers typically speak only French, Hausa or Zarma; contact your embassy for serious incidents.

avoid.reason: Avoid the river banks and city outskirts after dark and any travel beyond the city, as kidnapping and terrorism risks lead most governments to advise against travel to Niger.
Pickpocketing and bag snatching occur around the Grand Marché and Petit Marché; do not walk or drive at night and vary your routines.

hood_desc: The government and diplomatic quarter with the city's best hotels, restaurants, embassies and ministries; the safest, most convenient base for first-time visitors and business travelers.

A leafy riverside quarter along the Niger River near the Kennedy Bridge, prized for sunset views over the river and proximity to the National Museum; good for travelers wanting scenery and a quieter upscale stay.
A central, walkable quarter around the old railway terminus with a mix of guesthouses, bars and eateries; suited to budget and mid-range travelers who want to be near the action on foot.

The bustling area around the Grand Marché (Niamey's huge covered market), full of budget guesthouses, street food and local commerce; best for travelers wanting an immersive, low-cost stay near shopping.
A quieter residential and diplomatic area near the airport and Route de l'Aéroport, useful for early flights or longer stays needing calm surroundings.
lodging: Radisson Blu Hotel & Conference Center Niamey

water.note: Tap water is not recommended for visitors; use bottled or treated water.

transit.pay: Cash only (CFA francs) paid directly to the driver or conductor; there is no electronic fare card. Shared taxis are hailed on the street and shared with other passengers along fixed routes, with fares agreed or fixed per route; private taxi rides should be negotiated or fixed before departure since meters are not used.
transit.hours: Daytime service roughly 6am-8pm; very limited options after dark, so most visitors arrange private taxis or hotel transport at night.
transit.note: Niamey has no metro, tram or functioning passenger rail; a partially built rail line to Benin remains unused. Most visitors rely on taxis, hotel drivers, or private drivers rather than public buses.

bus: Intercity bush-taxis and coaches to Zinder, Maradi, Agadez
ferry: Seasonal pirogue (canoe) river crossings and tours on the Niger River

transit.m: Official airport taxi (fixed fare, prepay at counter)

tip.r: Not obligatory; rounding up or a small tip (a few hundred CFA) at restaurants is appreciated but not expected. Hotel porters may expect small change.

food.name: Riz sauce
food.desc: The national plate: a mound of rice under a slow-cooked sauce of tomato, onion and chilli, often thickened with peanut paste, with goat or beef.

places.name: Le Pilier
places.note: Long-standing Niamey restaurant whose rice with peanut sauce is a local favourite

places.name: Restaurant Baraka
places.note: Generous portions of traditional food at fair prices in a relaxed setting

places.name: Grand Marche food stalls
places.note: Cheapest and busiest place to eat riz sauce the way locals do at midday

food.name: Brochettes
food.desc: Skewers of beef or goat marinated in spice and grilled over open coals, dusted with chilli-peanut powder and finished with a squeeze of lime.

places.name: Plateau evening grills
places.note: Mobile grills appear on street corners after dark; the city's default evening meal

places.name: Grand Marche grill stalls
places.note: Vendors grilling to order beside the plantain fryers all afternoon

places.name: Le Gourmet
places.note: Smarter option for grilled lamb and beef if you want a table and a fan

food.name: Dambou
food.desc: Steamed maize or millet couscous tossed with shredded moringa leaves, black-eyed peas and a tomato-squash sauce - light, green and distinctly Nigerien.

places.name: Grand Marche cooked-food row
places.note: Women serve dambou from covered pots; ask for extra sauce and chilli

places.name: Restaurant Baraka
places.note: Keeps traditional grain and pulse dishes on the menu, not just grills

places.name: Petit Marche stalls
places.note: Small central market with a handful of home-cook stands doing dambou at lunch

food.name: Capitaine grille
food.desc: Nile perch from the river, split, salted and grilled whole over wood, served with raw onion, chilli and a wedge of lime on butcher paper.

places.name: Riverside fish grills, Kennedy Bridge
places.note: Plastic chairs on the sand at sunset; widely called the best meal in the city

places.name: Le Pilier
places.note: Serves river fish fillets alongside its French-influenced menu

places.name: Le Gourmet
places.note: Grilled fish done well indoors, with vegetarian sides available

food.name: Kilishi
food.desc: Beef pounded thin, coated in a peanut, chilli and spice paste and sun-dried into a sweet-hot jerky - the Sahel snack Niamey is known for.

places.name: Grand Marche kilishi sellers
places.note: Stacked sheets sold by weight; buy from a busy stall for the freshest batch

places.name: Wadata market
places.note: Neighbourhood market with kilishi makers drying meat in the open air

places.name: Marche Katako
places.note: Sprawling market where kilishi is sold alongside spices and dried goods

food.name: Masa
food.desc: Small fermented rice or millet cakes fried in a dimpled pan until puffed and lacy, eaten hot with chilli-peanut powder or a spoonful of sauce.

places.name: Grand Marche breakfast stalls
places.note: Pans going from first light; masa is the standard market breakfast

places.name: Marche Katako
places.note: Street cooks frying masa to order beside the tea sellers

places.name: Yantala roadside vendors
places.note: Residential-quarter stands serving masa and fried bean cakes in the morning

food.name: Foura
food.desc: Millet dough rolled into balls, crushed into soured milk and sweetened with sugar, ginger and spice - a thick, filling drink that doubles as lunch.

places.name: Grand Marche foura sellers
places.note: Women sell millet balls and milk from calabashes and mix it in front of you

places.name: Marche Katako
places.note: Cheap and cold; ask for less sugar if you want the sour milk to come through

places.name: Wadata market
places.note: Neighbourhood stands doing foura through the hottest part of the day

food.name: Bissap and ginger juice
food.desc: Hibiscus steeped with sugar and mint, or raw ginger blended with lime - both sold ice cold in bottles and frozen sachets across this alcohol-light city.

places.name: Grand Marche drink sellers
places.note: Coolers of bissap and ginger juice on every approach to the market

places.name: Le Pilier
places.note: House-made hibiscus and ginger juices served with the meal

places.name: Restaurant Baraka
places.note: Local juices offered as the standard non-alcoholic pairing

landmarks: Grande Mosquée de Niamey
This soaring mosque with its distinctive minaret dominates the Niamey skyline and offers sweeping panoramic views of the Niger River from its top.
Grand Marché de Niamey
A vibrant maze of stalls selling textiles, leatherwork, spices, and silver jewelry, this bustling market is the sensory heart of everyday Nigerien life.
Niger River waterfront
Golden sunsets over the wide Niger River, with fishermen in dugout canoes and grazing hippos nearby, make this riverside stretch endlessly photogenic.
Musée national Boubou-Hama
Niger's flagship national museum blends open-air pavilions, traditional architecture, and a small zoo, showcasing the country's history, crafts, and wildlife in one sprawling complex.
Pont Kennedy
Niamey's first bridge across the Niger River is a beloved city icon, linking the two banks and offering classic views of river life below.
Palais des Congrès de Niamey
This striking modernist convention hall, a gift from China, hosts state events and stands out as one of the capital's most architecturally bold landmarks.
Cathédrale Notre-Dame du Perpétuel Secours
Niamey's principal Catholic cathedral offers a striking contrast of quiet colonial-era architecture amid the bustling, predominantly Muslim capital.
Stade Général Seyni Kountché
Niger's national stadium is the electric epicenter of local football passion, drawing huge crowds and hosting the country's biggest sporting spectacles.
Deuxième Pont de Niamey (China-Niger Friendship Bridge)
This sleek, cable-stayed second bridge over the Niger River has become a modern symbol of the capital's growth, especially striking when lit at night.
National Assembly of Niger
The seat of Niger's parliament is a stately, guarded landmark whose grand facade reflects the ceremony and formality of national governance.

train.note: Niger has no operational passenger railway - the partly-built Niamey line to Dosso was never opened to regular service. All long-distance travel is by road.

intl.to: Ouagadougou (Burkina Faso), Bamako (Mali), Lome (Togo), Abidjan (Cote d'Ivoire) & Kano (Nigeria)

bus.note: RTV and the state operator SNTV run cross-border coaches from Niamey across West Africa. Borders are fluid: in mid-2026 the Niger-Benin border remains largely closed (so no Cotonou service) while the Nigeria border has reopened and Burkina Faso/Mali (AES) links run. Check travel advisories - parts of Niger carry serious security risks.

ferry.note: Landlocked. Only local pirogues (dugout canoes) cross the Niger River around Niamey; there are no scheduled ferry services.

full.name: Birnin Kebbi
full.blurb: Northwestern Nigerian city known for agriculture and its role as a regional capital.
